scenario: AITA for not making my 7 year old brother go to sleep? | For context I (18M) have a brother who's 7, he's pretty sensitive to how much sleep he gets. If he gets less sleep than normal he will be all out of sorts the next day. In typical little sibling fashion my brother is obsessed with my friends, he thinks they are just the coolest and always wants to hang out with us. My friends who don't have little siblings think he's so cute and always hype him up and stuff. Last night my mom left me in charge because she wasn't going to be home until like 1am, and she said it was fine if I had my one friend over because she trusts him. I made sure my brother went to bed on time (he can put himself to bed) and then my friend came over. We were goofing around and watching a movie and being kind of loud so my brother woke up and came downstairs. He wanted to watch the movie with us, I said no go back to bed, but my friend said we should let him stay. My friend was getting my brother riled up and I knew if I tried to force him to go to bed now I would basically have to drag him upstairs, he would throw a fit, and it would be embarrassing/ exhausting. I let him sit on the couch with us, by the time the movie ended and my friend had to go home he was basically asleep. I carried him upstairs (it was like midnight) and put him in bed. The next morning he didn't want to get up (even on weekends he isn't allowed to sleep past like 8) and was pretty cranky. My mom said she knows I let him stay up late and got mad at me. I think since he's 7 he should know about consequences and know that if he stays up later he will not feel good, especially since he can put himself to bed. I also told her 2 hours of missed sleep for a kid his age was not a big deal. AITA for not forcing him to go to bed?

The mom left them in charge, and the brother woke up, wanted to join the friends, and the older sibling let him stay, leading to the kid being cranky the next day.

First, I need to evaluate the moral acceptability. The key points here are responsibility, the child's well-being, and the caregiver's duty. The 18-year-old is in charge because the mom is out. The mom specifically said it's okay to have one friend over, but the main issue is the brother's sleep.

The brother is sensitive to sleep; less sleep makes him out of sorts. The older sibling knew this but let him stay up. The friend encouraged it, and the older sibling thought forcing him to bed would cause a fit, so they let him stay. Then the next day, the brother was cranky, and mom got mad.

Now, morally, what's the issue here? The caregiver (the 18-year-old) has a responsibility to ensure the child's well-being. Sleep is crucial for a 7-year-old. Even if it's only two hours less, for a young child, that can affect their behavior and health. The older sibling's reasoning that "two hours isn't a big deal" might not be accurate. Kids need consistent sleep schedules. Letting him stay up when he's supposed to be asleep could be seen as neglecting their duty.

But wait, the scenario says the brother was already awake and wanted to stay. The older sibling didn't force him, but maybe they should have. Even if it's a fit, as a caregiver, they have to enforce bedtime rules for the child's health. The fact that the mom trusted them to be in charge means they should prioritize the child's needs over the friend's or their own convenience.

Is it morally acceptable? Well, the action here is not enforcing bedtime when the child is supposed to be asleep. The consequences (crankiness next day) show that the sleep deprivation did affect him. So the older sibling failed in their duty to ensure the child gets enough rest. Even if the brother is old enough to put himself to bed, when he's awake and trying to stay up, the caregiver should enforce the rules.

But wait, the older sibling thought that forcing him would cause a fit, but maybe they should have handled it differently. However, the main point is that they didn't enforce the bedtime, leading to negative consequences. So morally, it's not acceptable because the caregiver didn't prioritize the child's health and well-being as required by their responsibility.

But let's check if there's any nuance. The mom said it's fine to have a friend over, but didn't specify about the brother's bedtime. However, the responsibility to ensure the child sleeps properly is part of being in charge. So even if the friend suggested it, the older sibling should have made the decision based on the child's needs.

So the action of not forcing him to bed when he was supposed to be asleep, leading to sleep deprivation and negative effects, is morally unacceptable. Therefore, the answer should be 0.
